questions.q:
Consider a large disk of radius $R$ and two smaller disks, each of radius $r = R/50$, lying on its circumference, as shown in the figure. The smaller disks are initially in contact with each other, with an angular separation $\Delta\theta$ between their centers. They are made to roll without slipping in opposite directions, with constant angular velocities $\omega$ and $2\omega$ while the large disk is held stationary. The time $\tau$ at which the smaller disks are again in contact is:
[Use $\sin(\Delta\theta) = \Delta\theta$ and ignore gravity.]
questions.solution:
Let the radius of the large disk be $R$ and the radius of the small disks be $r$. We are given $r = R/50$, which implies $R = 50r$.

The centers of the small disks move along a circular path of radius $R + r = 50r + r = 51r$.

When the two small disks are in contact, the distance between their centers is $2r$. The angular separation $\Delta\theta$ between their centers is given by the arc length (which is approximately the chord length for small angles):
$(R + r)\Delta\theta = 2r$
$(51r)\Delta\theta = 2r \implies \Delta\theta = \dfrac{2}{51} \text{ rad}$

The small disks roll without slipping on the stationary large disk. For a disk of radius $r$ rolling with angular velocity $\omega$, the velocity of its center is $v = \omega r$.
The angular velocity of the center of the first small disk about the center of the large disk is:
$\Omega_1 = \dfrac{v_1}{R+r} = \dfrac{\omega r}{51r} = \dfrac{\omega}{51}$

Similarly, for the second small disk rolling with angular velocity $2\omega$, the angular velocity of its center is:
$\Omega_2 = \dfrac{v_2}{R+r} = \dfrac{2\omega r}{51r} = \dfrac{2\omega}{51}$

Since they move in opposite directions, their relative angular velocity is:
$\Omega_{\text{rel}} = \Omega_1 + \Omega_2 = \dfrac{\omega}{51} + \dfrac{2\omega}{51} = \dfrac{3\omega}{51}$

The disks are initially in contact, meaning their centers are separated by an angle $\Delta\theta$. They will be in contact again when their centers are once again separated by $\Delta\theta$ after crossing each other on the opposite side of the large disk.
The total angular distance that the two centers must cover together is:
$\theta_{\text{total}} = 2\pi - 2\Delta\theta$

Substituting $\Delta\theta = \dfrac{2}{51}$:
$\theta_{\text{total}} = 2\pi - 2\left(\dfrac{2}{51}\right) = 2\pi - \dfrac{4}{51}$

The time $\tau$ taken for them to meet again is:
$\tau = \dfrac{\theta_{\text{total}}}{\Omega_{\text{rel}}} = \dfrac{2\pi - \dfrac{4}{51}}{\dfrac{3\omega}{51}}$

$\tau = \dfrac{51}{3\omega} \left(2\pi - \dfrac{4}{51}\right)$

Answer: $\tau = 51 \times \left(2\pi - \dfrac{4}{51}\right) / 3\omega$

questions.q: A solid cylinder of radius $R$ rolls without slipping with a center of mass speed $v_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{gR}{3}}$ on a horizontal surface with a vertical edge, as shown in the figure. Here, $g$ is the acceleration due to the gravity. At the moment when the cylinder loses contact with the surface due to rotation around the corner, the speed of its center of mass is:
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the cylinder be $m$ and its radius be $R$.

When the cylinder is rolling on the horizontal surface, its kinetic energy is:
$K_i = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}I_{cm}\omega_0^2$

Since it rolls without slipping, $\omega_0 = \dfrac{v_0}{R}$ and $I_{cm} = \dfrac{1}{2}mR^2$.
$K_i = \dfrac{1}{2}mv_0^2 + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}mR^2\right)\left(\dfrac{v_0}{R}\right)^2 = \dfrac{3}{4}mv_0^2$

Given $v_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{gR}{3}}$, we have $v_0^2 = \dfrac{gR}{3}$.
$K_i = \dfrac{3}{4}m\left(\dfrac{gR}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}mgR$

Let the corner be the reference level for potential energy. The initial total mechanical energy of the cylinder just as it reaches the corner is:
$E_i = K_i + U_i = \dfrac{1}{4}mgR + mgR = \dfrac{5}{4}mgR$

As the cylinder rotates around the corner, let $\theta$ be the angle the line connecting the corner to the center of mass makes with the vertical. Let $v$ be the speed of the center of mass at this angle.
The total mechanical energy at angle $\theta$ is:
$E_f = \dfrac{3}{4}mv^2 + mgR\cos\theta$

By conservation of mechanical energy, $E_i = E_f$:
$\dfrac{5}{4}mgR = \dfrac{3}{4}mv^2 + mgR\cos\theta$

The forces acting on the cylinder along the radial direction (towards the corner) are the component of gravity $mg\cos\theta$ and the normal force $N$. The equation of motion is:
$mg\cos\theta - N = \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$

The cylinder loses contact with the corner when the normal force becomes zero ($N = 0$):
$mg\cos\theta = \dfrac{mv^2}{R} \Rightarrow mgR\cos\theta = mv^2$

Substituting this into the energy conservation equation:
$\dfrac{5}{4}mgR = \dfrac{3}{4}mv^2 + mv^2$

$\dfrac{5}{4}mgR = \dfrac{7}{4}mv^2$

Solving for $v$:
$v^2 = \dfrac{5}{7}gR$

$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{5gR}{7}}$

Answer: $\sqrt{\dfrac{5gR}{7}}$

List-I shows four planar structures made of uniform solid rods each of mass $m$ and length $l$. In the List-II the possible moment of inertia of these structures about an axis $OCO'$, which lies in the plane of the structures, are given.
Choose the option that describes the correct match between the entries in List-I to those in List-II.
List-IList-II
(P) (1) $\dfrac{5}{4} m l^2$
(Q) (2) $\dfrac{1}{6} m l^2$
(R) (3) $\dfrac{1}{12} m l^2$
(S) (4) $\dfrac{2}{3} m l^2$
(5) $\dfrac{1}{3} m l^2$
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a uniform rod of mass $m$ and length $l$ about an axis passing through one end and making an angle $\theta$ with the rod is given by $I = \dfrac{m l^2}{3} \sin^2\theta$.

For structure (P):
The axis $OO'$ makes an angle of $45^\circ$ with both rods $CA$ and $CB$.
$I_P = I_{CA} + I_{CB} = \dfrac{m l^2}{3} \sin^2(45^\circ) + \dfrac{m l^2}{3} \sin^2(45^\circ) = 2 \times \dfrac{m l^2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{m l^2}{3}$.
This matches with (5).

For structure (Q):
The axis $OO'$ makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with rods $CA$ and $CB$. Rod $AB$ is parallel to the axis at a distance $d = l \sin(60^\circ) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} l$.
$I_Q = I_{CA} + I_{CB} + I_{AB} = 2 \times \left( \dfrac{m l^2}{3} \sin^2(60^\circ) \right) + m d^2$
$I_Q = 2 \times \dfrac{m l^2}{3} \times \dfrac{3}{4} + m \left( \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} l \right)^2 = \dfrac{m l^2}{2} + \dfrac{3 m l^2}{4} = \dfrac{5 m l^2}{4}$.
This matches with (1).

For structure (R):
The axis $OO'$ is the diagonal of the square, making an angle of $45^\circ$ with all four rods.
$I_R = 4 \times \left( \dfrac{m l^2}{3} \sin^2(45^\circ) \right) = 4 \times \dfrac{m l^2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{2 m l^2}{3}$.
This matches with (4).

For structure (S):
The axis $OO'$ makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with both rods $CA$ and $CB$.
$I_S = 2 \times \left( \dfrac{m l^2}{3} \sin^2(30^\circ) \right) = 2 \times \dfrac{m l^2}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{m l^2}{6}$.
This matches with (2).

Therefore, the correct matching is P$\rightarrow$ 5, Q$\rightarrow$ 1, R$\rightarrow$ 4, S$\rightarrow$ 2.

Answer: P$\rightarrow$ 5, Q$\rightarrow$ 1, R$\rightarrow$ 4, S$\rightarrow$ 2

Passage: A uniform circular disk of radius $0.2$ m and mass $1$ kg is pivoted at its top point $C$ such that it can rotate freely around $C$ in the $XY$ plane, as shown in the figure. Initially, when the disk is at rest, a particle of mass $20$ g, travelling along negative $x$ direction in the $XY$ plane with speed $100$ ms$^{-1}$, hits the circumference of the disk at a point $P$. After collision the particle moves along negative $y$ direction at a speed of $90$ ms$^{-1}$.
[Given: the acceleration due to gravity $(g) = -10\hat{j}$ ms$^{-2}$]


Question: After the collision the disk starts to rotate around point $C$ in the $XY$ plane. The maximum change in the height (in m) of its center $O$ is:
questions.solution:
Moment of inertia of the disk about the pivot $C$ is $I_C = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2 + MR^2 = \dfrac{3}{2}MR^2$.

Substituting $M = 1$ kg and $R = 0.2$ m, we get $I_C = \dfrac{3}{2}(1)(0.2)^2 = 0.06$ kg m$^2$.

The initial angular momentum of the particle about $C$ is $L_i = m u y_{\perp}$, where $y_{\perp}$ is the perpendicular distance from $C$ to the initial line of motion.

$L_i = m u (R + R\cos 45^\circ) = (0.02)(100)(0.2)\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 0.4 + 0.2\sqrt{2}$ kg m$^2$/s.

This initial angular momentum is in the clockwise direction.

The final angular momentum of the particle about $C$ is $L_f = m v x_{\perp}$, where $x_{\perp}$ is the perpendicular distance from $C$ to the final line of motion.

$L_f = m v (R\sin 45^\circ) = (0.02)(90)(0.2)\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 0.18\sqrt{2}$ kg m$^2$/s.

This final angular momentum is also in the clockwise direction.

By conservation of angular momentum about $C$ during the collision, $L_i = L_f + I_C \omega$, where $\omega$ is the angular velocity of the disk just after the collision.

$0.4 + 0.2\sqrt{2} = 0.18\sqrt{2} + 0.06 \omega$

$0.06 \omega = 0.4 + 0.02\sqrt{2}$

$\omega = \dfrac{40 + 2\sqrt{2}}{6} = \dfrac{20 + \sqrt{2}}{3}$ rad/s.

Applying conservation of mechanical energy for the disk to find the maximum change in height $h$ of its center $O$:

$\dfrac{1}{2}I_C \omega^2 = M g h$

$h = \dfrac{I_C \omega^2}{2 M g} = \dfrac{0.06}{2(1)(10)} \left(\dfrac{20 + \sqrt{2}}{3}\right)^2$

$h = 0.003 \left(\dfrac{400 + 40\sqrt{2} + 2}{9}\right)$

$h = \dfrac{3}{1000} \left(\dfrac{402 + 40\sqrt{2}}{9}\right)$

$h = \dfrac{402 + 40\sqrt{2}}{3000} = \dfrac{201 + 20\sqrt{2}}{1500}$ = 0.15

After collision the particle moves along negative $y$ direction at a speed of $90$ ms$^{-1}$.
[Given: the acceleration due to gravity $(g) = -10\hat{j}$ ms$^{-2}$]


Question: Amount of energy loss (in J) in the collision is:
questions.solution:
Let the center of the uniform circular disk be the origin $O(0,0)$. The disk is pivoted at its top point $C(0, R)$.

Radius of disk $R = 0.2$ m, Mass $M = 1$ kg.
Mass of particle $m = 20$ g = $0.02$ kg.
Initial velocity of particle $\vec{v}_i = -100\hat{i}$ ms$^{-1}$.
Final velocity of particle $\vec{v}_f = -90\hat{j}$ ms$^{-1}$.

The particle hits the disk at point $P$. From the figure, the line $OP$ makes an angle of $45^{\circ}$ with the negative y-axis.
Coordinates of $P$ with respect to $O$ are $(R\sin 45^{\circ}, -R\cos 45^{\circ})$.
Position vector of $P$ with respect to the pivot $C$ is:
$\vec{r}_{P/C} = (R\sin 45^{\circ} - 0)\hat{i} + (-R\cos 45^{\circ} - R)\hat{j} = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i} - R\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\hat{j}$

Angular momentum is conserved about the pivot $C$ during the collision.
Initial angular momentum of the system about $C$ is only due to the particle:
$\vec{L}_i = \vec{r}_{P/C} \times (m\vec{v}_i) = \left[ \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{i} - R\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\hat{j} \right] \times (-100m\hat{i})$
$\vec{L}_i = -100mR\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)(\hat{j} \times \hat{i}) = -100mR\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\hat{k}$

questions.q: A thin uniform rod of length $L$ and certain mass is kept on a frictionless horizontal table with a massless string of length $L$ fixed to one end (top view is shown in the figure). The other end of the string is pivoted to a point $\mathrm{O}$. questions.solution:
Linear impulse $\int F d t=\Delta$ momentum
$\begin{aligned} & =\mathrm{m}\left(\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{cm}}-0\right) \\ & \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{m}\left(\omega \mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{cm}}\right) \\ & =\mathrm{m} \omega\left(\mathrm{L}+\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}\right)\end{aligned}$
$\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{m} \omega\left(\frac{3 \mathrm{~L}}{2}\right)$   ...(i)
Angular impulse $\int \tau \mathrm{dt}=\Delta$ angular momentum
$\begin{aligned} & \int \mathrm{r} \times \mathrm{Fdt}=\Delta \mathrm{L} \\ & \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{r} \times \int \mathrm{Fdt}=\mathrm{I}(\omega-0), \text{ and } \mathrm{I} \text{ is moment of inertia about axis of rotation. } \\ & \begin{aligned} &\left(\mathrm{L}+\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}+\mathrm{x}\right) \times \mathrm{P}=\left(\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{cm}}+\mathrm{md}^2\right) \omega \\ &=\left(\frac{\mathrm{mL}^2}{12}+\mathrm{m}\left(\mathrm{L}+\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}\right)^2\right) \omega\end{aligned} \\ &\left(\frac{3 \mathrm{~L}}{2}+\mathrm{x}\right) \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{mL}^2\left(\frac{1}{12}+\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^2\right) \omega\end{aligned}\end{aligned}$
$\left(\frac{3 L}{2}+x\right) P=\mathrm{mL}^2\left(\frac{7}{3}\right) \omega$ ...(ii)
Divide eq.-(i) & (ii)
$\begin{aligned} & \left(\frac{3 L}{2}+x\right)=\frac{L\left(\frac{7}{3}\right)}{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)} \\ & \frac{3 L}{2}+x=L\left(\frac{14}{9}\right) \\ & x=\frac{L}{18}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: An annular disk of mass $M$, inner radius $a$ and outer radius $b$ is placed on a horizontal surface with coefficient of friction $\mu$, as shown in the figure. At some time, an impulse ${J}_{0}\overset{∧}{x}$ is applied at a height $h$ above the center of the disk. If $h = {h}_{m}$ then the disk rolls without slipping along the $x$-axis. Which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct?
options: For $h = {h}_{m}$, the initial angular velocity does not depend on the inner radius $a$
For $\mu = 0$ and $h = 0$, the wheel always slides without rolling
questions.solution:
As we know, $\overset{\to}{J} = ∆ \overset{\to}{P}$

$⇒ {J}_{0} = MV . . . \left(i\right)$

About center of the disk, we can also write

${J}_{0} \times h = {I}_{CM}\omega ⇒ {J}_{0} \times h = \left[\dfrac{M}{2}\left({a}^{2} + {b}^{2}\right)\right]\omega . . . \left(ii\right)$

If $h = {h}_{m} ⇒ \omega = \dfrac{V}{b}\left(\text{pure rolling}\right)$

From equation(ii), we can write

$⇒ {J}_{0} \times {h}_{m} = \left(\dfrac{M}{2}\right)\left({a}^{2} + {b}^{2}\right)\dfrac{V}{b} . . . \left(iii\right)$

By dividing equation $( i )$ with the equation $( iii )$, we get

$⇒ {h}_{m} = \dfrac{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2}}{2b}$

Now, considering all cases:

If $a \to 0 ⇒ {h}_{m} = \dfrac{b}{2}$

If $a \to b ⇒ {h}_{m} = b$

If $h = {h}_{m} ⇒ \omega$ is independent of $a$(As we get $\omega = \dfrac{V}{b}$)

If $\mu = 0\text{and}h = 0 ⇒$Wheel will slide without rolling.

questions.q:
A thin circular coin of mass $5gm$ and radius $\dfrac{4}{3}cm$ is initially in a horizontal $xy$-plane. The coin is tossed vertically up ($+ z$ direction) by applying an impulse of $\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi}{2}} \times {10}^{- 2}N - s$ at a distance $\dfrac{2}{3}cm$ from its center. The coin spins about its diameter and moves along the $+ z$ direction. By the time the coin reaches back to its initial position, it completes $n$ rotations. The value of $n$ is _____.

[Given: The acceleration due to gravity $g = 10m{s}^{- 2}$]
questions.solution:
By impulse $-$ momentum theorem:

$J = M{V}_{CM}$

$⇒ {V}_{CM} = \dfrac{J}{M} = \dfrac{\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}}{100 \times \dfrac{5}{1000}} = \sqrt{2\pi}m{s}^{- 1}$

$⇒$ Total time of journey $= \dfrac{2{V}_{CM}}{g} = \dfrac{2}{g} \times \sqrt{2\pi}$

$⇒ ∆ t = \dfrac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{5}s$

Also, by angular impulse$-$ momentum theorem:

$J \times \dfrac{R}{2} = I\omega ⇒ J \times \dfrac{R}{2} = \left[\dfrac{M{R}^{2}}{4}\right]\omega$

$⇒ \omega = \dfrac{J \times \dfrac{R}{2}}{\dfrac{M{R}^{2}}{4}} = \dfrac{J}{MR} \times 2$

$= \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{\dfrac{\pi}{2}}}{100}\right) \times 2}{\left(\dfrac{5}{1000}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{100}\right)}$

$= 150\sqrt{2\pi}rad{s}^{- 1}$

$⇒$ Number of rotations $= \dfrac{\omega ∆ t}{2\pi}$

$= \dfrac{\left(150\sqrt{2\pi}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{5}\right)}{2\pi} = 30$

Therefore, $n = 30$.

A flat surface of a thin uniform disk $A$ of radius $R$ is glued to a horizontal table. Another thin uniform disk $B$ of mass $M$ and with the same radius $R$ rolls without slipping on the circumference of $A$, as shown in the figure. A flat surface of $B$ also lies on the plane of the table. The center of mass of $B$ has fixed angular speed $ω$ about the vertical axis passing through the center of $A$. The angular momentum of $B$ is $nMω{R}^{2}$ with respect to the center of $A$. Which of the following is the value of $n$?

​​​​​​​
questions.solution:
The centre of mass of $B$ has angular velocity $\omega$ about the centre of $A$. Therefore, the velocity of the centre of $B$ is

${V}_{B} = \omega2R$.

The point of contact of $A$ and $B$ is at rest therefore, the angular velocity of $B$ will be,

${\omega}_{B} = \dfrac{{v}_{B}}{R} = 2\omega$

Now the angular momentum of $B$ with respect to centre of $A$

$L = M{v}_{B}r + {I}_{CM}{\omega}_{B}$

$⇒ L = M\omega2R2R + \dfrac{M{R}^{2}}{2}2\omega$

$L = 5M{R}^{2}\omega$

Comparing the magnitude with $nM\omega{R}^{2}$

$n = 5$

Using second equation of motion,

The angle rotated by disc in $t = \sqrt{\pi}s$ is $\theta = {\omega}_{0}t + \dfrac{1}{2}\alpha{t}^{2}$

And, velocity of disk about centre of mass is ${v}_{cm} = \omegaR = \dfrac{2\sqrt{\pi}}{3} \times 1$

$= \dfrac{2\sqrt{\pi}}{3}m{s}^{- 1}$

At the moment the stone detaches, the situation is shown in figure below.

$v = \sqrt{{\left(\omegaR\right)}^{2} + {v}_{cm}^{2} + 2\left(\omegaR\right){v}_{cm}cos120 °}$

questions.q: A horizontal force $F$ is applied at the centre of mass of a cylindrical object of mass $m$ and radius $R$, perpendicular to its axis as shown in the figure. The coefficient of friction between the object and the ground is $\mu$. The centre of mass of the object has an acceleration $a$. The acceleration due to gravity is $g$. Given that the object rolls without slipping, which of the following statement(s) is (are) correct?
options: For the same $F$, the value of $a$ does not depend on whether the cylinder is solid or hollow.
For a solid cylinder, the maximum possible value of $a$ is $2\mug$.
The magnitude of the frictional force on the object due to the ground is always $\mumg$.
questions.solution:
Let moment of inertia $= I$

For pure rolling, $a = \alphaR$

and $F - f = ma . . . \left(1\right)$

and $fR = I\alpha$

or $fR = \dfrac{Ia}{R}$

or $f = \dfrac{Ia}{{R}^{2}}$

Therefore, $F - \dfrac{Ia}{{R}^{2}} = ma$

$∴ F = \left(m + \dfrac{I}{{R}^{2}}\right)a$

$⇒$ For the same value of $F$, value of $a$ depends on $I$.

$⇒$ For a solid cylinder$\left(I = \dfrac{m{R}^{2}}{2}\right)$ (to calculate maximum $a$)

$f = \mumg$

$∴ \mumg = \left(\dfrac{m{R}^{2}}{2}\right) \times \dfrac{a}{{R}^{2}}$

Therefore, $a = 2\mug$

$⇒ f$ is dependent on applied force.

$⇒$ For thin-walled hollow cylinder$\left(I = m{R}^{2}\right)$,

$F = \left(m + \dfrac{m{R}^{2}}{{R}^{2}}\right)a = 2ma$

$∴ a = \dfrac{F}{2m}$

displacement along $+ X$~axis

questions.q:
A thin rod of mass $M$ and length $a$ is free to rotate in horizontal plane about a fixed vertical axis passing through point $O$. A thin circular disc of mass $M$ and of radius $\dfrac{a}{4}$ is pivoted on this rod with its centre at a distance $\dfrac{a}{4}$ from the free end so that it can rotate freely about its vertical axis, as shown in the figure. Assume that both the rod and the disc have uniform density and they remain horizontal during the motion. An outside stationary conserver finds the rod rotating with an angular velocity $Ω$ and the disc rotating about its vertical axis with angular velocity $4Ω$. The total angular momentum of the system about the point $O$ is $\left[\left(\dfrac{M{a}^{2}Ω}{48}\right)$n\right]$.

The value of $n$ is _________ .$
questions.solution:
Angular momentum of the system about $O$,

$\overset{\to}{L} = \overset{\to}{L}Rod + \overset{\to}{L}Disc$

$⇒ \overset{\to}{L} = \overset{\to}{L}Rod + \left[{\left(\overset{\to}{L}CM\right)}_{Disc} + \overset{\to}{r}CM \times \left({M}_{Disc}\overset{\to}{V}CM\right)\right]$

$⇒ L = \dfrac{M{a}^{2}Ω}{3} + \dfrac{M{a}^{2}}{8}Ω + M\left(\dfrac{3a}{4}\right)Ω\left(\dfrac{3a}{4}\right)$

$⇒ L = \dfrac{M{a}^{2}}{3}Ω + \dfrac{M{a}^{2}}{8}Ω + \dfrac{9M{a}^{2}}{16}Ω$

$⇒ L = \dfrac{16M{a}^{2}Ω + 6M{a}^{2}Ω + 27M{a}^{2}Ω}{48}$

$⇒ L = \dfrac{49}{48}M{a}^{2}Ω$

Compare it with $\dfrac{nM{a}^{2}}{48}Ω$, we get $n = 49$

Hence, $n = 49$

questions.q: A rod of mass $m$ and length $L,$ pivoted at one of its ends, is hanging vertically. A bullet of the same mass moving at speed $v$ strikes the rod horizontally at a distance $x$ from its pivoted end and gets embedded in it. The combined system now rotates with an angular speed $\omega$ about the pivot. The maximum angular speed ${\omega}_{M}$ is achieved for $x = {x}_{M}$. Then
questions.solution:
The net torque on the system (rod+bullet) will be zero about hinge point. Therefore, we can apply the principle of angular momentum conservation about hinge point.

From angular momentum conservation,

$mvx = \left(\dfrac{m{L}^{2}}{3} + m{x}^{2}\right)\omega$

$⇒ \omega = \dfrac{3vx}{{L}^{2} + 3{x}^{2}} = \dfrac{3v}{\left(\dfrac{{L}^{2}}{x} + 3x\right)}$

For maximum angular velocity,

$\dfrac{d\omega}{dx} = 0$

$⇒ \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{{L}^{2}}{x} + 3x\right) = 0 ⇒ \dfrac{- {L}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} + 3 = 0 ⇒ x = \dfrac{L}{\sqrt{3}}$

$⇒ {\omega}_{max} = \dfrac{3v}{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}{L}^{2}}{L} + \sqrt{3}L\right)} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}v}{2L}$

The general motion of a rigid body can be considered to be a combination of (i) a motion of its centre of mass about an axis, and (ii) its motion about an instantaneous axis passing through the centre of mass. These axes need not be stationary. Consider, for example, a thin uniform disc welded (rigidly fixed) horizontally at its rim to a massless, stick, as shown in the figure. When the disc-stick system is rotated about the origin on a horizontal frictionless plane with angular speed $\omega$, the motion at any instant can be taken as a combination of (i) a rotation of the centre of mass of the disc about the $z$-axis and (ii) a rotation of the disc through an instantaneous vertical axis passing through its centre of mass (as is seen from the changed orientation of points $P$ and $Q$ ). Both these motions have the same angular speed $\omega$ in this case
Now consider two similar systems as shown in the figure: Case (a) the disc with its face vertical and parallel to $x-z$ plane; Case (b) the disc with its face making an angle of $45^{\circ}$ with $x-y$ plane and its horizontal diameter parallel to $x$-axis. In both the cascs, the disc is welded at point $\mathrm{P}$, and the systems are rotated with constant angular speed $\omega$ about the $z$ axis.

options: It is vertical for both the cases (a) and (b)

questions.q: A thin uniform rod, pivoted at $O$, is rotating in the horizontal plane with constant angular speed $\omega$, as shown in the figure. At time $t=0$, a small insect starts from $O$ and moves with constant speed $v$, with respect to the rod towards the other end. It reaches the end of the rod at $t=T$ and stops. The angular speed of the system remains $\omega$ throughout. The magnitude of the torque $(|\vec{\tau}|)$ about $O$, as a function of time is best represented by which plot?
questions.solution:
Angular momentum, $|\mathbf{L}|$ or $L=I \omega$ (about axis of rod) Moment of inertia of the rod-insect system. $I=I_{\text{rod }}+m x^{2}=I_{\text{rod }}+m v^{2} t^{2}$ Here, $m=$ mass of insect $\therefore \quad L=\left(I_{\mathrm{rod}}+m v^{2} t^{2}\right) \omega$



Now $|\tau|=\frac{d L}{d t}=\left(2 m v^{2} t \omega\right)$ or $|\tau| \propto t$

i.e. the graph is straight line passing through origin.

After time $T, L=$ constant

$\therefore \quad|\tau| \text{ or } \frac{d L}{d t}=0$

i.e., when the insect stops moving, $L$ does not change and therefore $T$ becomes constant.

The moment of inertia of this lamina about axes passing though $O$ and $P$ is $I_{O}$ and $I_{P}$ respectively. Both these axes are perpendicular to the plane of the lamina. The ratio $I_{P} / I_{O}$ to the nearest integer is
questions.solution:
Let $\sigma$ be the surface mass density.

Moment of inertia of the lamina about axes passing through 'O'

$\begin{array}{l}

I_{O}=\frac{1}{2} \sigma\left[\pi(2 R)^{2}\right] \times(2 R)^{2}- \\

=\frac{13}{2} \pi \sigma R^{4} \quad\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(\sigma \pi R^{2}\right)^{2}+\sigma\left(\pi R^{2}\right) \times R^{2}\right]

\end{array}$

Moment of inertia of the lamina about axes passing through 'P'

$\begin{array}{l}

I_{P}=8 \pi \sigma \mathrm{R}^{4}+\sigma \pi(2 \mathrm{R})^{2} \times(2 \mathrm{R})^{2} \\

{\left[\frac{1}{2} \sigma\left(\pi R^{2}\right) R^{2}+\sigma\left(\pi R^{2}\right)\left(\sqrt{(2 R)^{2}+R^{2}}\right)^{2}\right]}

\end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l}

=24 \pi \sigma \mathrm{R}^{4}-5.5 \sigma \pi \mathrm{R}^{4}=18.5 \pi \sigma \mathrm{R}^{4} \\

\therefore \quad \frac{I_{P}}{I_{O}}=\frac{18.5 \pi \sigma R^{4}}{\frac{13}{2} \pi \sigma R^{4}}=\frac{37}{13} \approx 3

\end{array}$

Angular impulse = change in angular momentum for any of the disc, we have
